reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: A collection of pus in the pleural cavity, most commonly a complication of bacterial pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion progressing to empyema)
In children the typical picture is persistent fever, cough, tachypnoea, and pleuritic chest pain despite appropriate antibiotics for pneumonia
The process evolves through an exudative stage, a fibrinopurulent stage with loculations, and finally an organising stage with a thick fibrous peel restricting the lung
Clinical findings include reduced chest expansion, dullness to percussion, and diminished breath sounds over the effusion
Ultrasound is valuable for confirming and characterising the collection, detecting loculations, and guiding drainage

Management combines appropriate antibiotics with drainage; chest tube insertion, sometimes with intrapleural fibrinolytics, is used, and thoracoscopic (VATS) debridement may be needed for organised, loculated disease
Late organising empyema with a thick peel trapping the lung may require decortication to allow re-expansion
Common causative organisms in children include Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus
reference.pathophysiology: Thoracic empyema usually develops when a bacterial pneumonia extends to the pleura, producing an initially free-flowing exudate that becomes infected and purulent. Fibrin deposition then creates loculations that compartmentalise the pus (fibrinopurulent stage), and if untreated, fibroblast proliferation forms a thick inelastic peel over the visceral pleura (organising stage) that traps and restricts the underlying lung. Less commonly empyema follows chest trauma, surgery, or spread from mediastinal or subphrenic infection. The trapped infection sustains sepsis and impairs ventilation of the affected lung.
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph to identify pleural fluid and its extent
Pleural ultrasound to confirm the collection, assess loculation, and guide drainage
Contrast CT of the chest in complex or non-resolving cases
Pleural fluid analysis with Gram stain, culture, cell count, pH, and biochemistry
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers, and testing for tuberculosis where relevant
redFlags: Sepsis or septic shock from ongoing pleural infection requiring urgent resuscitation and source control
Respiratory distress from a large effusion compressing the lung
Persistent high fever and clinical deterioration despite antibiotics, indicating inadequate drainage
Features suggesting a bronchopleural fistula or necrotising pneumonia
reference.prognosis: With prompt antibiotics and adequate drainage most children recover fully with good long-term lung function. Delayed or inadequate drainage prolongs illness and may require more invasive surgery such as decortication, but even organised empyema in children generally has a favourable long-term outlook once treated.
pitfalls: Relying on antibiotics alone and delaying drainage of an established empyema
Attempting simple aspiration or a single small drain for heavily loculated collections
Missing an underlying necrotising pneumonia, tuberculosis, or bronchopleural fistula
Failing to recognise a trapped lung requiring surgical decortication
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
